newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo wages up but poverty still widespread -report.
newsitem.headline: Yugo wages up but poverty still widespread -report.

text.p: Yugoslavs earned on average 10 percent more in June than in May, but economists said on Tuesday that 57 percent of the workforce was still facing poverty.

The average wage in the public sector reached 807 dinars ($103) in June, with industry workers receiving 684 dinars and non-industry employees 1,256 dinars, the IZIT Institute for Market Research said in its latest report.
Low wages in various industry sectors, still performing at below 60 percent of their capacities, resulted from a huge surplus labour burden.
"Average June wages were 10 percent up on May and 24.9 percent up on June 1996 in real terms," Tomislav Milisavljevic of the the Belgrade-based IZIT told a news conference.
But he cautioned the numbers were misleading due to a "defective" methodology used to calculate the average monthly income.

Yugoslavia's statisticians changed the methodology earlier this year to include the total workforce, regardless of whether they all received salaries. The change was needed to lower the base used to calculate pensions.

Although the average purchasing power of Yugoslavs in June was 10 percent up on May and 17.3 percent up on the same month last year in real terms, the average wage remained insufficient to cover half of a basket of basic foodstuffs costing 1,558 dinars for a four-member family.
The gap between the lowest and highest wages narrowed to 11.4 times from 15.77 times in May. The lowest wage in June stood at 194 dinars and the highest at 2,216 dinars.
Central bank employees, workers in the oil and gas sector, business associations, insurance and air-traffic were among the top paid Yugoslavs.

Yugoslavia has 2.013 million employed but 154,200 of them received wages below the minimum 200 dinars. Those working in the leather and textile industries need up to 11 wages for a monthly food-basket encompassing 65 staples.
IZIT researchers said 57.2 percent or 1.153 million Yugoslavs lived on wages below the average, while 19.5 percent lived below subsistence levels. Wages are frequently several months late.
Around 393,804 Yugoslavs, working in the recycling, wood processing, leather and fur production and construction industries, live on 50 percent of the average wage.
Another 759,804 Yugoslavs or 37.7 percent of the total employed, receive between half and full average wage.
Around 7.4 percent live on two average wages, while 157,379 working for insurance companies, health sector, business associations and oil and gas industry earn 2.5 times the average.
Only 0.6 percent or 13,244 working in the central bank and oil industry receive three average wages. -- Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 311 4254
